newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. concerned over Japan economic growth--Mondale.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned over Japan economic growth--Mondale.

text.p: The United States is concerned about the strength of Japan's economic growth, because a slowdown would dampen Japan's appetite for imports and affect trade and current account balances, outgoing U.S. ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale told a news conference on Tuesday.
Mondale is set to leave Japan later this month, ending a 3-1/2 year term to return to private law practice.

"One of the problems right now is we're not sure how strong Japan's economic growth pattern is," Mondale said. "The last few months it's been better but you get conflicting reports about the next year or so."
"If Japan slips off its growth pattern it will import less and the current account and trade balances will be affected," Mondale said. "We are concerned about that."

Mondale said U.S.-Japan economic ties had improved and progress had been made in reducing Japan's overall current account surplus as well as America's bilateral deficit with Japan during his tenure as envoy. "While the weaker yen may reverse some of these trends, and we can't be complacent, I believe important progress has been made," he said.
But he added that Japan's market remained "vastly over-regulated" and that only limited progress in deregulation had been made.

Mondale said he was concerned that the need to overcome resistance to deregulation from vested interests such as bureaucrats and affected businesses would "continue to frustrate efforts to open the Japanese economy".
But he also said there was a new "sense of urgency" within Japan about the need to deregulate to stay competitive globally.
"I think there are a lot of things coming together here that may bring about a more decisive result on demands for deregulation than in the past," he said.

Mondale welcomed progress in using the trade dispute settlement mechanisms of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), but added: "This does not mean, however, that the age of bilateralism is over" in U.S.-Japan economic relations.
He said many areas such as anti-competitive practices, telecommunications and financial services were not yet covered by the WTO.
"As the world's two largest economies, the United States and Japan require a very active bilateral dialogue," he said.
"For some time yet, there are many areas where we will have no other alternative but the bilateral one."
